learning.title: A derived expectation needs a swap test; repetition only proves stability
learning.trigger: A test computes its expected value from the data it just wrote - `a.id < b.id ? [x, y] : [y, x]`, an index arithmetic, a hand-rolled tie-break - instead of naming a literal.
learning.symptom: The assertion fails every run in the same direction, or passes every run, and nobody can tell whether the derivation is right. Running it again changes nothing, so the team concludes the assertion is fine ("it's stable") or files it as flake. Both are wrong: a derivation can be stable and reversed.
learning.rule: For every conditional that derives an expected value, swap the two inputs and require the output to swap. A reversed ternary returns the same wrong order both ways and fails instantly. This is a ten-second check with no database, no fixture and no run. Apply it to every derivation in the file, not only the one that failed.

Two green runs prove an ORDER-SENSITIVE assertion is stable. They say nothing about whether a DERIVATION is correct, because an always-inverted conditional fails identically on every run. Stability and correctness are different questions, and a repeat-until-green discipline answers only the first.
Do not paper over a derivation with a sleep or a forced-distinct timestamp. Separating the rows in time hides the class and the next person copying the case inherits the weakness.
learning.evidence: PR 540, `tests/integration/read-the-tickets-linked-to-one-task_test.ts`. `const linksOfSecond = otherLinkId < secondLinkId ? [otherTask, taskId] : [taskId, otherTask]` returned the tasks backwards in BOTH branches, because the read answers newest first and the larger id leads, so the branch that assumed that returned the smaller id's task first. Modelled over 200,000 random pairs it was wrong in 200,000 of them: red by construction, not a coin flip. It read as flake because two runs failed with opposite orderings as the random ids differed per run. Four reviewers including the author re-read the line and passed it. The swap test would have caught it in seconds. Raised by qa-qa after she saw the pattern in two red runs; fixed in `0c88bf1aa` and replaced entirely in `985e34d1d` once the real ordering rule was read from source.
